differences.title: 1. INDEXING MODEL
differences.leftDesc: Meilisearch builds and updates indexes through configurable ingestion settings, favoring quick indexing and predictable latencies. Updates are applied in batches, then background refresh makes new documents searchable.
differences.rightDesc: Elasticsearch splits indexes into shards, writing documents into Lucene segments. Each refresh publishes new segments to search; merges later compact segments to reduce overhead and improve query efficiency.

differences.title: 2. RELEVANCE CONTROLS
differences.leftDesc: Meilisearch exposes ranking rules and facets with a straightforward API, making it easy to tune typo tolerance, searchable attributes, and ranking factors without building complex query DSL. Defaults are optimized for fast iteration.
differences.rightDesc: Elasticsearch offers a full Query DSL backed by Lucene scoring, including BM25 variants, field boosts, function_score, script_score, and rescoring. This enables deep relevance engineering across many query shapes.

differences.title: 3. QUERY EXECUTION
differences.leftDesc: Meilisearch primarily targets full-text and lexical retrieval with fast response times, executing optimized inverted-index lookups. Its API encourages single-purpose search endpoints with consistent performance characteristics.
differences.rightDesc: Elasticsearch executes queries across shards, merges top-k results, and can run compound queries (bool, dis_max), aggregations, and filters. Coordination overhead grows with cluster size and query complexity.

differences.title: 4. FACETS & AGGREGATIONS
differences.leftDesc: Meilisearch supports facets tailored for common filtering and navigation, returning distribution counts alongside hits. It’s designed for predictable, developer-friendly facet usage with less query authoring than general-purpose aggregation trees.
differences.rightDesc: Elasticsearch includes a comprehensive aggregations framework (bucket, metric, pipeline). It builds aggregation trees per shard and reduces results centrally, enabling complex analytics within the same request as search.

differences.title: 5. SCHEMAS & MAPPING
differences.leftDesc: Meilisearch uses dynamic, developer-controlled settings and primarily relies on JSON attributes as fields, reducing friction. You can configure searchable and filterable attributes without the heavy mapping lifecycle typical of Elasticsearch.
differences.rightDesc: Elasticsearch requires mappings defining field types, analyzers, and indexing options. Correct mappings are critical because changing field types later often requires reindexing, especially for text analysis and keyword behaviors.

differences.title: 6. SCALING & OPERATIONS
differences.leftDesc: Meilisearch is typically operated as a simpler service with fewer moving parts. Scaling usually means adding replicas/instances and relying on built-in mechanisms for consistency and predictable resource usage.
differences.rightDesc: Elasticsearch scaling involves tuning shard counts, replicas, refresh intervals, merge policies, and allocation settings. Operational tasks include ILM, snapshot/restore, and monitoring resource hotspots across nodes and shards.

differences.title: 7. ECOSYSTEM & EXTENSIBILITY
differences.leftDesc: Meilisearch prioritizes straightforward lexical retrieval features with a compact surface area, making it easier to integrate quickly. Extensibility exists, but complex analytics/search workflows may require external orchestration.
differences.rightDesc: Elasticsearch has a large ecosystem: ingest pipelines, enrich processors, transforms, integrations, and extensive plugin options. This supports end-to-end search-and-observability pipelines (often with Kibana).
